start.title: New to tinnitus? Start here
start.metaTitle: New to Tinnitus? What to Do First, and What to Expect | Tinnitus Evidence
start.metaDesc: Just noticed ringing in your ears? What helps in the first days and weeks, the few warning signs that need quick help, and an honest answer to whether it goes away.
start.lead: Hearing a sound no one else can hear can be frightening, especially at first. You are not alone: about 1 in 7 adults has some tinnitus,[[jarach]] and it is usually not a sign of anything serious.[[nhs]]
start.nowTitle: If it has just started, here's what helps first
now: Check the few warning signs. Sudden hearing loss, tinnitus after a head injury, new tinnitus that beats with your pulse, weakness in your face or severe dizziness need medical help quickly. When to get help quickly
Book a check with a doctor or an audiologist (a hearing specialist). A hearing test is the usual first step, and simple causes such as earwax or an ear infection can be treated.[[aao,nice]]
Tonight, avoid total silence. A soft sound you like, such as a fan or quiet music, can make the ringing less noticeable.[[nhs]] Help for difficult nights
Go easy on yourself. Worry and stress can make tinnitus more noticeable.[[nhs]] Feeling alarmed by a new sound is a normal reaction, and it often settles as the sound becomes familiar.
Hold off on buying "cures". No pill, supplement or device has been shown to switch tinnitus off.[[nidcd,aao]] Before you spend money
start.nowFoot: Feeling desperate or unsafe? Talk to someone now. For tinnitus advice, Tinnitus UK's free helpline (0800 018 0527) is open Monday to Friday, 10am to 4pm UK time.

sections.title: The few signs that need quick help
sections.intro: Most tinnitus can wait for a routine appointment. A few situations can't:[[nhs,nice]]

summary.emergency: sudden weakness in the face, arm or leg, trouble speaking or seeing, severe spinning dizziness that won't settle, or tinnitus after a recent head injury.
summary.today: a sudden drop in hearing (even if it started days or a few weeks ago), or new tinnitus that beats with your pulse and came on suddenly.
summary.soon: tinnitus in one ear only, pulsing tinnitus that has been there a while, or tinnitus that is affecting your sleep or mood.

sections.title: What tinnitus is
sections.html:
Tinnitus means hearing a sound, such as ringing, buzzing, hissing or humming, that doesn't come from outside you. It is a symptom, not a disease.[[aao]]

It can follow loud noise, or come with hearing loss, an ear infection or earwax. Some medicines can cause it, and sometimes there's no clear reason.[[nidcd]] Most people with tinnitus have some hearing loss, which a hearing test can show.[[aao]] Stress doesn't usually cause tinnitus, but it can make it more noticeable.[[nhs]]

A sudden ringing in one ear that fades within about 5 minutes is different. The main US tinnitus guideline doesn't cover it, because it doesn't usually need medical care.[[aao]]

sections.title: The first few weeks: what helps
sections.html:
• Use sound, not silence. Quiet rooms make tinnitus stand out. Low background sound, such as a fan, the radio or nature sounds, gives your ears something else to hear.[[nhs]]
  • Protect your ears from loud noise, but not from everyday sound. Wear earplugs at concerts or with power tools. In one trial at a music festival, 12% of people wearing earplugs had new tinnitus afterwards, against 40% without.[[ramakers]] But try not to block out ordinary sounds. Wearing earplugs for long stretches can make everyday sounds seem too loud.[[tukhyper,ata,munro]]
  • Look after your sleep. Tinnitus and poor sleep often go together. Sleep and difficult nights has practical steps for tonight and the longer term.
  • Keep doing the things you enjoy. Absorbing activities give your attention somewhere else to go. Try not to spend long periods listening for the sound.[[nhs]]
  • Be careful with forums and videos. Talking with others can help you feel less alone, but some online spaces are full of worst-case stories and conflicting advice.[[ainscough]] If reading makes you more frightened, take a break.
  • If you take a medicine you think might be linked, don't stop it on your own. Ask the person who prescribed it.

If tinnitus is bothering you, or affecting your sleep or mood, you don't have to wait months to ask for help.[[ata,nice]]

sections.title: Will it go away? An honest answer
sections.html:
Some tinnitus goes away, especially soon after it starts, but often it doesn't. Even when the sound stays, it often becomes less of a problem, and there is help for that.

  • Soon after it starts: two small studies followed people who saw an ear specialist in the first month. About 1 to 2 in 10 had no tinnitus 6 months later.[[wallhausser,vielsmeier]] People whose tinnitus faded quickly may never have seen a specialist, so the real chance may be higher.
  • Tinnitus that has been there a while: a large UK study followed adults aged 40 to 69. About 2 in 10 no longer had it 4 years later. Of those who still had it, most said it was about the same; about 1 in 10 said it was better and 1 in 10 worse.[[dawes]]
  • How much it bothers people: on average this eases a little over time, though it varies a lot from person to person.[[phillips]] Talking therapies such as CBT (cognitive behavioural therapy) can reduce its impact on daily life.[[cochrane_cbt]]

We can't promise that it will fade, or that everyone gets used to it, and anyone who promises either is guessing. What we can say is that there are ways to manage tinnitus that help many people live well with it.[[nice]] The full evidence: does tinnitus go away?

sections.title: Before you spend money
sections.html:
Tinnitus attracts a lot of marketing, and it is natural to want a quick fix. Leading guidelines advise against these as tinnitus treatments:

  • Dietary supplements, such as ginkgo, zinc or vitamin blends sold for tinnitus.[[aao]] The evidence
  • Betahistine, a medicine sometimes prescribed for tinnitus or dizziness.[[nice]]
  • Hearing aids if your hearing test shows no hearing loss. They are a good option when there is hearing loss.[[nice]]
  • Antidepressants, anti-seizure or anti-anxiety medicines as a routine tinnitus treatment. They may still be right for you for other reasons, such as low mood.[[aao]]
  • rTMS (magnetic brain stimulation).[[aao]] The evidence

Expensive sound gadgets aren't proven to work better than a fan, a radio or a free app. The UK guideline found too little evidence to recommend any particular sound therapy.[[nice]] If something promises a cure, check the claim or look it up in Emerging and unproven treatments.

sections.title: Seeing a doctor about it
sections.html:
A family doctor (GP) or an audiologist is usually the first step. It helps to say clearly what is happening. For example:

  • "It started on [date], in [one / both] ears."
  • "It does / doesn't beat in time with my pulse."
  • "My hearing has / hasn't changed, and I do / don't feel dizzy."
  • "It's affecting my sleep / mood / work."
  • "Could I have a hearing test?"

If you're told nothing can be done, that usually means there's no cure, not that nothing can help. It's fine to ask about support for sleep and distress, or for a referral or second opinion.[[ata]] Prepare for your appointment has a notes sheet you can fill in and print.

sections.intro: Tick off what you've done. Print it or save it as a PDF if that helps.

evidence.text: A hearing test (audiological assessment) is recommended for people with tinnitus.[[aao,nice]]
Talking therapy based on CBT is recommended for tinnitus that keeps bothering you. It reduces the impact on daily life, not the sound itself; the evidence is rated low certainty.[[aao,cochrane_cbt]]
Supplements, betahistine and rTMS are advised against as tinnitus treatments.[[aao,nice]]
Earplugs at a loud music festival reduced new tinnitus afterwards (12% vs 40%).[[ramakers]]
Background sound is an option in the US guideline, but the UK guideline found too little evidence to recommend it. Many people find it comforting.[[aao,nice,nhs]]
Keeping busy, limiting time on forums, and not over-using earplugs are expert advice with little direct research.[[ata,tukhyper,ainscough]]

sleep.title: Sleep and difficult nights
sleep.metaTitle: Tinnitus and Sleep: What Helps Tonight and in the Long Run | Tinnitus Evidence
sleep.metaDesc: Can't sleep because of tinnitus? What to do right now, how to use sound at night, what to do after a bad night, and the treatment with the best evidence for long-term sleep problems.
sleep.lead: Tinnitus often seems louder at night and in the early morning,[[probst]] and around half of people with tinnitus say they sleep poorly.[[gu]] If you're reading this awake, you're not alone, and there are things that can help.
sleep.nowTitle: Having a difficult night? Try this now
now: Put on a soft, steady sound you like, such as a fan, rain or low music. Keep it a little quieter than your tinnitus: it doesn't have to cover it.[[tuksound]]
Let yourself rest. You don't have to force sleep; resting in bed is still helpful.[[tuksleep]]

If you've been wide awake for what feels like 20 to 30 minutes (guess, don't check the clock), get up and do something calm in dim light. Go back to bed when you feel sleepy.[[aasm2021,tuksleep]] Take care on the stairs in the dark.
When you've finished reading, put your phone face down, or set a timer on your bedtime sound.
If you feel desperate tonight, you don't have to cope alone. Talk to someone now
sleep.nowFoot: One bad night is hard, but it is usually nothing to worry about. Take extra care tomorrow if you need to drive and feel very drowsy.

sections.title: Using sound at night
sections.html:
A quiet bedroom makes tinnitus stand out. Gentle background sound gives your ears something else to hear.[[tuksleep]]

  • Choose something pleasant that doesn't demand attention: a fan, rain, waves, soft music or a quiet radio. If a sound annoys you, try another.[[tuksound]]
  • Keep the volume low, a little quieter than your tinnitus, so you can still just hear it. Very loud sound can give relief in the moment, but the tinnitus may seem louder when it stops.[[tuksound]]
  • Timer or all night? Either is fine. A timer suits you if you mainly struggle to fall asleep. Leaving a soft sound on helps if you wake in the early hours.[[tuksound]]
  • Use a bedside speaker or a pillow speaker rather than earbuds all night, and keep it at a gentle level. A pillow speaker is quieter for a partner.[[tuksound]]

On an iPhone: Settings, then Accessibility, Audio & Visual, Background Sounds. Choose rain, ocean or another sound, set the volume, and use the timer if you like. If you want the sound to keep playing with the screen locked, turn off Stop Sounds When Locked.[[apple]]

Sound can make nights more comfortable. It hasn't been shown to reduce tinnitus over time, and expensive devices aren't proven to do better than a fan or a free app.[[cochrane_sound,nice]]

sections.title: If your mind is racing
sections.html:
• Try a worry list earlier in the evening. Spend 15 to 20 minutes writing down what's on your mind and what you could do about it. Worries are then less likely to arrive at bedtime.[[tuksleep]]
  • Give yourself an hour to wind down before bed, away from work and bright screens.[[tuksleep,nhs_insomnia]]
  • Keep the bed for sleep. If you can't sleep, get up for a while rather than lying there getting frustrated.[[aasm2021]]
  • Relaxation can help, such as slow breathing or relaxing your muscles one group at a time.[[aasm2021]]

sections.title: Tomorrow, after a bad night
sections.html:
• Get up at your usual time, even after a poor night. Sleeping in can make the next night harder.[[nhs_insomnia,aasm2021]]
  • Avoid long naps. If you must nap, keep it short and early in the day.[[aasm2021,tuksleep]]
  • Stay active in the day, but not with hard exercise close to bedtime.[[tuksleep]]
  • Go easy on caffeine and alcohol. Avoid tea, coffee and alcohol for about 6 hours before bed. Alcohol and over-the-counter sleep aids can make you wake earlier.[[nhs_insomnia,tuksleep]]
  • Be careful driving if you feel very sleepy.

sections.title: If poor sleep has gone on for a while: CBT for insomnia
sections.html:
CBT for insomnia (CBT-I) is the recommended first treatment for long-term insomnia. It suits people with other health conditions too, and it can be done online.[[aasm2021,acp,euro2023]] It is a short course that changes the habits and worries that keep poor sleep going.

In people with tinnitus, the early evidence is encouraging. In one trial, more than 8 in 10 people who had CBT-I said their sleep clearly improved. That compared with 47% in an audiology-based sleep programme and 20% in a support group. Their tinnitus distress fell too.[[marks]] A review of four smaller trials found sleep improved on average.[[curtis]]

What it's like

It usually takes several weeks. You may feel more tired at first, especially if it includes "sleep restriction": spending less time in bed for a while, so that sleep becomes deeper. If you drive for work, or have bipolar disorder or seizures, do that part with a clinician.[[aasm2021]] CBT-I: our evidence page

Where to find it

  • UK: ask your GP. NICE recommends the digital programme Sleepio; in England whether it's offered depends on your local NHS area, and it's free for adults in Scotland.[[htg624,parl]]
  • US: the VA's free Insomnia Coach app is a self-help programme based on CBT-I, available to everyone.[[insomniacoach]] (The VA's CBT-i Coach app is meant to be used with a therapist.) SleepioRx is an FDA-cleared digital CBT-I programme; ask your doctor.[[fda]] Sleep specialists who offer CBT-I are listed by the Society of Behavioral Sleep Medicine.
  • Australia: the free online THIS WAY UP Insomnia Program, which you can do on your own or with a clinician.[[thiswayup]]
  • Elsewhere: ask your doctor about CBT-I, including online CBT-I.

See a doctor before starting a self-help programme if you snore loudly, stop breathing in your sleep or feel very sleepy in the day. The same goes if you have bipolar disorder or seizures, or are at risk of falls.[[insomniacoach,htg624]]

sections.title: Sleeping tablets and melatonin
sections.html:
• Sleeping tablets are only for short-term use, usually a few days or weeks. They can have serious side effects and you can become dependent on them.[[nhs_insomnia,euro2023]] If you already take them, don't stop suddenly: talk to your prescriber first.
  • Melatonin doesn't treat tinnitus.[[s3]] For sleep, US sleep specialists advise against it for long-term insomnia.[[aasm2017]] In the UK it's prescription-only, and mainly for short-term use in people aged 55 and over.[[nhs_melatonin]] Supplements sold in the US are often wrongly labelled.[[jama2023]] Ask a doctor before trying it. Supplements: the evidence
  • Other medicines, such as antidepressants, aren't a routine treatment for tinnitus itself. A doctor may still use them for sleep or mood problems.[[aao,s3]]

sections.title: When to talk to a doctor, and what to say
sections.html:
If poor sleep happens on 3 or more nights a week for 3 months or more and affects your days, doctors call it long-term insomnia.[[aasm2017,nhs_insomnia]] You don't have to wait that long: see a doctor sooner if it's making it hard to cope.[[nhs_insomnia]]

You could say: "Tinnitus is stopping me sleeping on [number] nights a week, for [weeks or months]. It's affecting my [work / mood / concentration]. Could you check my sleep, for example with the Insomnia Severity Index, and refer me for CBT-I?"[[nice]]

Also mention loud snoring, gasping in your sleep or feeling very sleepy in the day. These can be signs of sleep apnoea, when breathing stops and starts during sleep, which is treatable.[[htg624]]

Keep a simple sleep diary for a week or two: when you went to bed, roughly when you fell asleep, when you woke and when you got up. It helps your doctor see the pattern.[[euro2023]] Prepare for your appointment

sections.title: Your calmer-night plan
sections.intro: Pick the steps that suit you. Tick them off, print them, or keep this page open by the bed.
items: Choose a soft bedtime sound, and set it a little quieter than my tinnitus
Write a worry list earlier in the evening
Wind down for an hour before bed
No tea, coffee or alcohol in the 6 hours before bed
If I'm wide awake for a while, get up and do something calm, then go back to bed
Get up at the same time every morning, even after a bad night
Keep naps short and early, or skip them
If this has gone on for weeks, ask a doctor about CBT for insomnia

evidence.text: CBT for insomnia is the recommended first treatment for long-term insomnia in adults, including online CBT-I.[[aasm2021,acp,euro2023]]
In people with tinnitus, CBT-I improved sleep in one 102-person trial and, on average, in a review of four small trials.[[marks,curtis]]

Getting up when you can't sleep, keeping a regular wake-up time, and relaxation are recommended parts of insomnia treatment. Sleep tips on their own aren't recommended as the main treatment.[[aasm2021]]
Gentle sound is an option in the US tinnitus guideline. Studies haven't shown that sound devices reduce tinnitus over time, and none measured sleep.[[aao,cochrane_sound]]
Sound volume, worry lists and phone habits are expert advice from tinnitus charities, with little direct research.[[tuksound,tuksleep]]

appointment.title: Prepare for your appointment
appointment.metaTitle: Tinnitus Appointment: What to Say, Ask and Expect | Tinnitus Evidence
appointment.metaDesc: Seeing a doctor or audiologist about tinnitus? A notes sheet you can fill in and print, questions to ask, what a hearing test is like, and what to do if you're told nothing can be done.
appointment.lead: A family doctor or an audiologist (a hearing specialist) is usually the first step.[[nidcd,aaocare]] A little preparation helps you get the most from a short appointment, and leave with a plan.
now: Start with how it affects you, in one sentence. For example: "Tinnitus is stopping me sleeping, and I've had to cut back at work." Doctors often interrupt within seconds, so say the most important thing first.[[singh,aao]]
Say why you're coming now, especially if you've had it a while.[[nice]]
Bring notes. Fill in the notes sheet below, and list your medicines and supplements.[[ahrq]]
Choose your top 3 questions from the list below.[[ahrq,sansoni]]
Bring someone if you can. A second pair of ears helps you remember what was said.[[wolff]]
appointment.nowFoot: Sudden hearing loss, new pulsing tinnitus or tinnitus after a head injury shouldn't wait for a routine appointment. When to get help quickly

sections.title: Who to see first
sections.html:
• US: your primary care doctor, or an audiologist for a full hearing test.[[nidcd,aaocare]] On Medicare you can see an audiologist once a year without a referral for gradual hearing changes; other insurance varies.[[asha_medicare]]
  • UK: your GP. They can check your ears and refer you for a free NHS hearing test.[[nhs,nhs_tests]] Some areas let you refer yourself to NHS audiology.
  • Australia: your GP.[[healthdirect]]
  • Elsewhere: your family doctor.

In the US and thinking about over-the-counter hearing aids? See a doctor first if your tinnitus is only in one ear, or your hearing changed suddenly.[[fda_otc]]

sections.title: Your notes to take
sections.intro: Type here, or print it and write by hand. Skip anything that doesn't apply. These are the things you'll usually be asked about.[[aaoehr,nice]]

fields.label: How it affects me
fields.hint: Sleep, focus, mood, work. A score from 0 to 10 is fine.

fields.label: When it started
fields.hint: Roughly when, and whether it came on suddenly or slowly.

fields.label: Where I hear it, and what it sounds like
fields.hint: One ear, both, or in my head. Ringing, buzzing, hissing? Always there, or comes and goes?

fields.label: Does it beat in time with my heartbeat?
fields.hint: If yes: is it louder when I exercise? Any headaches or eyesight changes?

fields.label: Does it change when I move my jaw, head or neck?
My hearing and ears
fields.hint: Hearing loss, a blocked feeling, ear pain or discharge, sounds seeming too loud.

fields.label: Anything that happened around the start
fields.hint: Loud noise, an ear infection, a cold, a head injury or whiplash.

fields.label: Sleep
fields.hint: Trouble getting to sleep or staying asleep? Loud snoring or gasping at night?

fields.label: Medicines and supplements
fields.hint: Include when you started each one. Don't stop a prescribed medicine without asking.

fields.label: What I've tried, and what helped

sections.html:
• What might be causing my tinnitus? Do I have any hearing loss?
  • Do I need any other tests? Why, or why not?
  • Would hearing aids help me?
  • What help is there for sleep, stress or low mood? Can I be referred for CBT?
  • What can I do about sounds that feel too loud?
  • When should I protect my ears?
  • What should make me come back sooner?
  • What's the next step if this doesn't help?

sections.title: Before you leave
sections.html:
• Check you've understood: "So the next step is... is that right?" Saying it back helps you remember.[[talevski]]
  • Ask who will contact whom, how long it might take, and what should make you come back sooner.
  • Ask for a copy of your hearing test and any written information.[[nice,ahrq]] You have a right to see your health records.[[hipaa]]
  • Afterwards, jot down what was found and what was suggested, while it's fresh.

sections.title: What to expect
sections.html:
Good tinnitus care usually includes:

  • Questions about your tinnitus and your health, and a look in your ears.[[aao]]
  • A full hearing test.[[aao,nice]]
  • Questions about how much it bothers you, your sleep and your mood.[[aao,nice]]
  • An explanation of what tinnitus is and what can help, and a plan you agree on.[[aao,nice]]
  • Hearing aids if you have hearing loss, or a cochlear implant assessment if it is severe.[[aao]]
  • CBT, a talking therapy that helps you cope, if tinnitus keeps affecting your life. In the UK it's often offered online first.[[aao,nice,nhs]]
  • A follow-up to see how you're doing.[[aao]]

Questions about your mood are normal

You may be asked how you're feeling, and whether you've had thoughts of harming yourself. This is routine for anyone bothered by tinnitus, and it's safe to answer honestly. It helps your clinician find the right support.[[aao,aaomh]] Struggling now? Support and crisis lines

What usually isn't needed

A scan. Most people with tinnitus don't need one. Scans are for specific signs, such as tinnitus in one ear only, tinnitus that pulses, or new symptoms like weakness or numbness.[[aao,aaopatient,nice]]

Medicines or supplements for the tinnitus itself. They aren't recommended, although medicines may still help with sleep, anxiety or low mood.[[aao]]

If your tinnitus changes when you move your jaw, head or neck, mention it. Some people are referred to a physiotherapist or dentist to check for a jaw or neck problem; the evidence that this helps is limited.[[aao,aaocare]] Read more

sections.title: What a hearing test is like
sections.html:
A hearing test is painless. It usually takes 15 minutes to an hour, and you often get the results the same day.[[nhs_tests]]

  • Audiogram (the main hearing test): you wear headphones and press a button whenever you hear a beep, even a very faint one.[[nhs_tests,bsa]]
  • Speech test: the same idea, with words instead of beeps.[[nhs_tests]]
  • Middle-ear check (tympanometry): a soft tip rests in your ear for a few seconds to see how well your eardrum moves. Not everyone needs it.[[nhs_tests,nice]]
  • A short questionnaire about how tinnitus affects you.[[nice]]

Tips for test day

  • If loud sounds bother you, say so before you start. You can ask them to begin quietly, and you can stop at any time.[[aazh,bsa]]
  • If you can't tell the beeps from your tinnitus, tell the tester. They can use a different kind of tone.[[bsa]]
  • Ask for a copy of your results.

Some clinics also try to match the pitch and loudness of your tinnitus. UK guidance doesn't recommend this, so don't worry if it isn't done.[[nice]]

sections.title: If you're told "nothing can be done"
sections.html:
There's no cure yet, but there is help. Advice, hearing care and CBT help many people feel better, even when the sound stays the same.[[aao,aaopatient,nice]] Tinnitus charities advise doctors not to tell patients that nothing can be done.[[tukgp]]

You could say: "I understand there's no cure yet. I'd like help with how it's affecting my sleep and mood. Could I have a full hearing test, and talk about options like CBT or a referral to audiology?"

If it still bothers you after this first advice, UK guidance says you should be referred for specialist tinnitus care.[[nice]] You can also ask to see another doctor.[[rnid]]

sections.title: When it shouldn't wait for an appointment
sections.intro: Get help sooner than a routine appointment if you have:[[nhs,nice]]

summary.emergency: sudden weakness in the face, arm or leg, trouble speaking or seeing, severe spinning dizziness that won't settle, or tinnitus after a recent head injury.
summary.today: a sudden drop in hearing (even if it started days or a few weeks ago), or new tinnitus that beats with your pulse and came on suddenly.
summary.soon: tinnitus in one ear only, pulsing tinnitus that has been there a while (ask for an urgent appointment), or hearing that is getting worse.

evidence.text: Clinicians should find out how much tinnitus bothers you. If it does, they should ask about your mood and any thoughts of self-harm.[[aao]]
Everyone with tinnitus should be offered a full hearing test. CBT is recommended if tinnitus keeps bothering you.[[aao,nice]]
Most people with tinnitus don't need a scan unless there are specific warning signs.[[aao,nice]]
A list of questions can help people ask more and get more information. Bringing someone along is linked to longer visits and more information, with mixed results.[[sansoni,wolff]]
About 1 in 5 people seeking help for tinnitus or sound sensitivity found standard test sounds uncomfortable, so asking to start quietly is reasonable.[[aazh]]
Leading with the impact and saying why you're coming now are practical tips, based on what guidelines ask clinicians to explore.[[nice,singh]]

overwhelmed.title: When it feels like too much
overwhelmed.metaTitle: When Tinnitus Feels Like Too Much: Support and Help That Works | Tinnitus Evidence
overwhelmed.metaDesc: Struggling to cope with tinnitus? Where to talk to someone now, small steps that help today, the talking therapies with the best evidence, and how to reach them where you live.
overwhelmed.lead: Living with a sound you can't switch off can be exhausting. If it feels like too much right now, you're not alone, and with the right help it can get easier.
now: If you're thinking about suicide, or feel you can't keep yourself safe, please talk to someone now. The lines below are free and confidential. Crisis lines
Take a few slow breaths, or try 5 to 10 minutes of relaxation. Relaxation helped people in a tinnitus trial.[[mckenna,nhs]]
Give your attention somewhere gentle to go: a sound you like, a short walk, or something that absorbs you.[[nhs]]
Tell someone you trust how you're feeling, or call a tinnitus helpline when it's open.[[nhs]] Tinnitus helplines
Be kind to yourself. Feeling this way is common, it isn't a personal failing, and it can ease.[[salazar,cochrane_cbt]]
overwhelmed.nowFoot: Not in danger, but worn down? That's very common. Small steps that help are just below the helplines.

sections.title: Talk to someone now
sections.intro: These services are free, confidential and staffed by trained people. You don't have to be in crisis to call. Not in danger right now? Skip to small steps

sections.title: What you may be feeling
sections.html:
Many people with tinnitus feel anxious, low, angry or hopeless at times, especially when sleep suffers. In studies of people seeking help for tinnitus, around 1 in 3 had depression, and anxiety is common too.[[salazar,pattyn]]

Feeling this way doesn't mean you've failed to cope. It means you need, and deserve, support.

sections.title: Small steps that help
sections.html:
• Plan one small, enjoyable thing each day, and gently return to things you've stopped doing because of tinnitus. Planning pleasant activities is a recommended way to ease low mood.[[nice_dep,ptm_wb]]
  • Keep doing what matters to you, with short breaks rather than pushing through.
  • Move your body. Gentle exercise, especially with others, can help with low mood.[[nice_dep]]
  • Practise relaxation, such as slow breathing or relaxing your muscles one by one.[[nhs,mckenna]]
  • Look after your sleep. Everything feels harder after bad nights. Sleep and difficult nights
  • Take breaks from forums and from searching for cures. Some people leave online forums feeling there is no help, which isn't true.[[budimir]]
  • Connect with people who understand. Many people say tinnitus support groups help them feel less alone and more hopeful.[[pryce,nhs]] Support organizations

sections.title: Help that works: talking therapies
sections.html:
CBT is the best-supported help for tinnitus distress, and US, UK and European guidelines recommend it.[[aao,nice,cochrane_cbt]] CBT (cognitive behavioural therapy) is a talking therapy. It helps you change the thoughts and habits that make tinnitus harder to live with. On average it reduces how much tinnitus affects daily life and mood, though it usually doesn't change the sound itself.[[cochrane_cbt]]

Online CBT with some support from a therapist or audiologist also helps many people. In one trial it worked about as well as group CBT.[[sattel,jasper]] Two related therapies, acceptance and commitment therapy (ACT) and mindfulness-based therapy (MBCT), have also helped in smaller trials.[[westin,mckenna]]

CBT · Online CBT · ACT · MBCT: the evidence

sections.title: How to get CBT-based help where you live
sections.html:
• UK: ask your GP. You'll usually be offered online CBT first.[[nhs,nice]] In England you can also refer yourself to NHS Talking Therapies for anxiety or low mood, including when you have a long-term condition. It's for adults, and it's general support, not tinnitus-specific.[[talking]] Is distress stopping you doing your usual daily activities, even after first support? Then NICE says you should be referred and seen within 2 weeks. You can ask your GP about this.[[nice]]
  • US: ask your doctor or an audiologist about CBT-based tinnitus care. The American Tinnitus Association's directory lists local providers, but it doesn't check them. Ask whether they offer CBT-based tinnitus care.[[ata_dir]] The ABCT finder lists CBT therapists (top listings are paid).[[abct]] Veterans can ask VA audiology about Progressive Tinnitus Management.[[ptm_rct]]
  • Australia: if tinnitus has led to depression or anxiety, your usual GP can make a Mental Health Treatment Plan. Medicare then covers up to 10 individual and 10 group sessions a year.[[betteraccess]] MindSpot offers free online courses.[[mindspot]]
  • Canada: in Ontario, Ontario Structured Psychotherapy offers free CBT for depression and anxiety.[[ontario]] Elsewhere, ask your family doctor.
  • Germany: Kalmeda is a tinnitus CBT app in the official DiGA directory. A doctor can prescribe it, and statutory health insurance pays.[[diga]]

Free places to start

  • The Living Better with Tinnitus workbook (US VA and Department of Defense), free for anyone, covering sound, pleasant activities, relaxation and balancing thoughts.[[ptm_wb]]
  • Tinnitus UK's free Take on Tinnitus online course. It hasn't been formally evaluated.[[tot]]

sections.title: Before you spend money
sections.html:
When you feel desperate, offers of a cure can be very tempting. Before you pay for anything, ask:

  1. Has it been tested against a placebo or sham treatment in people with tinnitus? Check a claim
  2. Do guidelines advise against it? Supplements, rTMS, betahistine, and medicines used to treat the tinnitus itself are advised against.[[aao,nice]]
  3. Are there warning signs? "Miracle cure", "all natural", one product that does it all, quick fixes, glowing testimonials, or claims that doctors are hiding it.[[fda_fraud]]
  4. Is there a big upfront cost or subscription with no trial or refund?
  5. What does your doctor or audiologist think? Free, guideline-backed help (talking therapy, sound, hearing aids if you have hearing loss) comes first.[[fda_fraud,aao]]

Emerging, experimental and unproven treatments

sections.title: When to get more help
sections.html:
If tinnitus is affecting your mood, sleep or work most days, tell your doctor. You can say: "It's affecting my mental health." You may be asked about your mood and whether you've had thoughts of harming yourself. That's routine, and it's safe to answer honestly.[[aao]] Prepare for your appointment

If you feel you can't keep yourself safe, use the lines above now.

evidence.text: CBT is recommended by US, UK and European guidelines for tinnitus that keeps bothering you. The evidence is low certainty, and most studies follow people only to the end of treatment.[[aao,nice,cochrane_cbt]]
Online CBT with support from a therapist or audiologist helps many people, though many studies had high drop-out.[[sattel,jasper]]
ACT and mindfulness-based therapy (MBCT) helped in single trials of 64 and 75 people.[[westin,mckenna]]
Planning activities and group exercise are recommended for less severe depression in general.[[nice_dep]]
Many people describe support groups as helping them feel connected and hopeful; this hasn't been measured as an outcome.[[pryce]]
Taking breaks from forums, pacing yourself and the support plan are expert advice with little direct research.[[budimir]]

concentration.title: Concentration, work and study
concentration.metaTitle: Tinnitus and Concentration: Practical Help at Work and Study | Tinnitus Evidence
concentration.metaDesc: Finding it hard to focus with tinnitus? Practical steps for work and study, how to ask for adjustments, safe headphone use, and noise at work, with the research explained.
concentration.lead: If tinnitus makes it harder to focus, you're not imagining it: many people with tinnitus find concentration harder, and studies back this up.[[tegg,clarke]] Small, practical changes often help.
now: Use low, steady background sound while you work, such as a fan, gentle music or nature sounds, a little quieter than your tinnitus.[[tuksound]] Treat it as a tool you can use when it helps, not something you must always have on.[[hesser]]
Do your hardest task at your best time of day, and break long tasks into shorter chunks.
Take short, regular breaks. Trying to push through for hours tends to raise stress.[[tukself]]
Choose a quieter seat, away from printers, busy walkways or rattling air vents, if you can.[[jan]]
Look after your sleep. Tiredness makes focusing much harder. Help for difficult nights
concentration.nowFoot: If you strain to follow conversations, a hearing check is worth booking: hearing difficulties can drain concentration more than tinnitus itself.[[waechter,fuel]] Prepare for your appointment

sections.title: At work
sections.html:
• Background sound at your desk: a quiet fan or a low, pleasant sound through one earbud or a small speaker.[[tuksound,jan]]
  • Meetings and video calls: turn on captions, sit where you can see faces, and ask for written notes afterwards.[[jan]]
  • Noise-cancelling headphones can help you keep the volume low in noisy places.[[who]] If you use them to block office chatter, play a soft sound through them. Total silence can make tinnitus more noticeable.
  • On a headset all day? Keep the volume below about 60% of maximum and give your ears breaks between calls.[[who]]

Asking for changes

Small adjustments are often easy for an employer: a quieter desk, a sound machine, flexible hours or home working, spread-out breaks, captions in meetings.[[jan,acas]] You don't have to tell anyone about your tinnitus unless you want to.[[acas]]

You could say: "I have tinnitus, a constant sound in my ears. It can make concentrating harder in quiet rooms or long meetings. A few small changes help me, such as [a quieter desk with low background sound / captions in meetings / short breaks / some home working]. Could we try them for a month and review?" Keep a note of what you agree.

  • US: you can ask in plain words; you don't need to say "ADA" or "reasonable accommodation".[[eeoc]] Concentrating and hearing count as major life activities under the ADA.[[ada]] The free Job Accommodation Network lists ideas for tinnitus.[[jan]]
  • UK: if tinnitus has a big, long-term effect on daily life, it can count as a disability under the Equality Act. Your employer must then make reasonable adjustments.[[gov_equality,acas]] Acas has a free template letter for asking. Access to Work can fund extra support, but not the adjustments your employer must make by law.[[atw]] (Northern Ireland has different rules.)

sections.title: At college or university
sections.html:
• Contact disability or student support services early. Colleges and universities must make reasonable adjustments, and you usually need to ask.[[gov_equality]]
  • Ask what is available, such as recorded lectures, note-taking support, seating near the front, or a quieter room for exams.
  • In England, Disabled Students' Allowance can pay for equipment or support after a needs assessment.[[dsa]]
  • Study in short blocks with breaks, with low background sound rather than silence.[[tuksound,tukself]]

sections.title: If your work is noisy
sections.html:
Did your tinnitus start or get worse with noise at work? Tell your employer, and ask about a noise assessment, hearing protection and hearing checks. Above certain noise levels these are legal duties.[[hse,osha]]

  • UK: from 80 dB(A), your employer must assess the risk and give you hearing protection if you ask. From 85 dB(A), protection must be provided and worn. People who already have hearing loss may need regular hearing checks.[[hse]]
  • US: from 85 dBA averaged over a workday, employers must provide free hearing protection and yearly hearing tests.[[osha]]

For music and other listening, the World Health Organization's safe level for adults is about 80 dB for up to 40 hours a week. Louder sound means less time.[[who]]

sections.title: Why focusing can feel harder
sections.html:
Studies find small-to-moderate links between tinnitus and three things: holding your attention, switching between tasks, and thinking quickly on hard tasks.[[tegg,clarke]] One explanation is that the sound competes for your attention. These are links, not proof that tinnitus causes the difficulty. Many people with tinnitus do just as well as anyone else.[[clarke]]

Other things often play a part, and most of them can be helped: hearing loss (listening takes more effort),[[waechter,fuel]] poor sleep, stress, anxiety and low mood.[[tegg]]

sections.title: If it keeps affecting your work or study
sections.html:
• Get a hearing check. If you have hearing loss, even mild, hearing aids can make listening easier.[[nice,tukhear]] Hearing aids: the evidence
  • Treat poor sleep. CBT for insomnia has the best evidence for long-term sleep problems.[[curtis]] CBT-I: the evidence
  • Consider CBT for tinnitus. It can reduce how much tinnitus interferes with daily life, and it's available online. Evidence on work and concentration specifically is limited.[[cochrane_cbt,beukes]] CBT · Online CBT

evidence.text: Reviews find small-to-moderate links between tinnitus and attention, task-switching and processing speed. They are associations, not proof of cause.[[tegg,clarke]]

Hearing aids are recommended when hearing loss affects communication, and CBT for tinnitus that keeps bothering you.[[nice,cochrane_cbt]]
Safe listening (about 80 dB for up to 40 hours a week) and noise-at-work duties come from the WHO and national regulators.[[who,hse,osha]]

Background sound, breaks, quieter seating and the manager script are expert advice with little direct research. Trying to control every sound can backfire, so use sound flexibly.[[tuksound,jan,hesser]]

spikes.title: Spikes and difficult days
spikes.metaTitle: Tinnitus Spikes: What to Do When It Suddenly Gets Louder | Tinnitus Evidence
spikes.metaDesc: Tinnitus louder than usual today? A quick check for the rare changes that need help, what to do right now, common triggers (and the coffee myth), and when to get checked.
spikes.lead: Tinnitus often goes up and down: most people who seek help say theirs varies.[[devos]] A louder spell can be frightening, but it often eases back towards your usual level.
now: Do a quick check. Has your hearing suddenly dropped? Is there new dizziness, weakness in your face, or a recent head injury? Is it newly beating with your pulse? If yes, get checked today. If not, this sounds like an ordinary spike.[[nhs]]
Add gentle sound. Quiet rooms are the most common thing people say makes tinnitus worse.[[pan]] A fan, music or the radio at a low level can take the edge off.[[nhs]]
Slow your breathing, or try a short relaxation exercise. Stress and tinnitus often rise and fall together.[[goldberg,nhs]]
Give your attention somewhere else: a walk, a phone call, a task that absorbs you. Try not to keep checking whether it's still there.[[nhs,tuktame]]
Keep your plans, at a gentler pace. Avoiding things can make tinnitus feel more important.[[tuktame,tukself]]
spikes.nowFoot: If it feels like too much, you don't have to cope alone. Talk to someone now

sections.title: Will it settle?
sections.html:
For most people, tinnitus goes up and down. A louder spell often eases back towards your usual level, sometimes within hours, sometimes over a few days.[[goldberg,simoes]] Researchers haven't yet measured exactly how long spikes last, and they can be hard to predict.[[engelke]]

It's also common for tinnitus to seem louder at night or first thing in the morning.[[probst]] And a lasting change is less common than you might fear: in a large UK study, most people said their tinnitus bothered them about the same amount 4 years later.[[dawes]]

A few words to tell yourself

"This is a spike. I've had louder days before, and they've eased. A louder day doesn't usually mean something is wrong. I don't need to keep checking it. I'll put on some gentle sound and do one small thing I enjoy."

Noticing a worried thought and answering it kindly is a technique from CBT.[[tukstress]]

sections.title: What people often notice before a spike
sections.html:
What goes with louder days differs from person to person.[[simoes,pan]] Things people often mention:

  • Quiet rooms, and bedtime.[[pan]]
  • Stress or worry.[[pan,goldberg]]
  • A poor night's sleep.[[pan]] Help for difficult nights
  • Loud noise, such as a concert or power tools.[[pan]]
  • A cold or other illness, or ears blocked with wax.[[beukes,nidcd]]
  • A new medicine. Ask your pharmacist or doctor, and don't stop a prescribed medicine on your own.

What about coffee? Studies haven't found that caffeine makes tinnitus worse.[[stclaire,glicksman]] Stopping suddenly can cause headaches, so keep your usual amount steady. It can still affect sleep, so go easy in the evening.[[tukfood]]

And alcohol? It affects people differently: in one study, most noticed no change.[[pugh]]

sections.title: After a loud event
sections.html:
Ringing after a concert or other loud noise usually fades by the next day.[[ata]] Dull or muffled hearing after loud noise often recovers within a day or two.[[nidcd_nihl]] If your hearing still feels reduced after that, or drops suddenly, get it checked the same day. Even when it settles, it's a sign your ears needed protecting.[[nidcd_nihl]]

Carry earplugs for loud places. But don't wear them in everyday quiet, because that can make you more sensitive to sound.[[nhs_hyper]]

sections.title: When a change needs checking
sections.intro: Most spikes aren't a sign of anything serious. Get help if a change comes with any of these:[[nhs,nice]]

summary.emergency: tinnitus after a head injury, or with weakness in your face, arm or leg, trouble speaking, or severe spinning dizziness that won't settle.
summary.today: a sudden drop in hearing, hearing that hasn't recovered a day or two after loud noise, or new tinnitus that beats with your pulse.
summary.soon: a spike that keeps getting worse or hasn't started to ease after about a week, a change in one ear only, or tinnitus that is affecting your sleep or mood.

sections.title: If spikes keep coming
sections.html:
• Try a simple spike diary for 2 to 4 weeks, filled in once a day, then stop. Note how intrusive it was (0 to 10), how you slept, stress, loud noise, illness and any new medicine. Look for your own pattern, and test one suspected trigger at a time.[[tukfood]] Keep it short: in one study, half of people noticed their tinnitus more while tracking it.[[goldberg]]
  • See your doctor for a check-up and a hearing test if spikes are frequent and you can't work out why.[[nhs]]
  • Get longer-term help. CBT, a talking therapy, can reduce how much tinnitus affects your life.[[cochrane_cbt]] CBT: the evidence

sections.title: Your spike plan
sections.intro: Keep this for your next louder day. Print it or save it as a PDF if that helps.
items: Do the quick check: no sudden hearing loss, new dizziness, weakness, head injury or new pulsing
Put on gentle sound
Take a few slow breaths, or do a short relaxation
Read my few words to myself
Do one absorbing thing
Keep my plans, at a gentler pace
Protect my ears only in genuinely loud places
If it hasn't started to ease after about a week, book an appointment

evidence.text: Tinnitus loudness and bother go up and down within the same person, and tend to move together with stress.[[goldberg,simoes,devos]]
How long spikes last, and how often they return to baseline, hasn't been studied.[[engelke]]
Cutting out caffeine didn't help tinnitus in a blinded trial, and caused withdrawal symptoms.[[stclaire]]
Avoid total silence, try relaxation, don't focus on the sound, and don't wear earplugs all the time.[[nhs,nhs_hyper]]
CBT may reduce the impact of tinnitus on daily life.[[cochrane_cbt]]
The quick check, the words to tell yourself, the spike plan and the diary are practical tools built from expert advice; they haven't been tested as such.[[tukstress,tukfood,tuktame]]

spikes.evidenceNote: Most of what we know about spikes comes from people rating their tinnitus on their phones through the day. It shows patterns, not causes.

family.tileDesc: Explaining tinnitus, and how loved ones can help
family.title: Family and relationships
family.metaTitle: Tinnitus and Family: How to Explain It and How Loved Ones Can Help | Tinnitus Evidence
family.metaDesc: Tinnitus affects the whole household. A 30-second way to explain it, what helps and what doesn't for partners and family, home tips, children, and what to do if you're worried.
family.lead: Tinnitus doesn't only affect the person who hears it. Partners and families often feel it too, and couples often don't talk about it.[[beukes22,mancini18]] A few simple conversations can make home life easier for everyone.
family.nowTitle: Three things to try this week
now: Explain it in 30 seconds. For example: "I hear a sound no one else can hear. It isn't dangerous. On bad days it makes me tired and short-tempered, and that isn't about you. What helps most is ___."
Say what helps. People with tinnitus often say they want others to take it seriously, face them when talking, and accept background sound at night.[[mancini18,mancini19]]
Agree some ground rules for talking about it: when to talk, how you'll say it's a bad day (a code word works), and what would help then.[[tukpartner]]
family.nowFoot: Worried about someone's mood or safety? What to do if you're worried

sections.title: For partners and family: what helps
sections.html:
Usually helps

  • Listen and believe them. Tinnitus is real, even though you can't hear it.
  • Ask what would help, such as choosing a quieter or less echoey place to meet.[[tukpartner,tukfriend]]
  • Keep doing things together, and gently encourage them not to give up things they enjoy.[[tukpartner]]
  • Be patient. Getting used to tinnitus often takes months.[[ata_love]]
  • Go to an appointment with them if they'd like you to.[[mancini18]]
  • Wear earplugs with them at loud events.[[tukpartner]]
  • Look after yourself too.[[tukpartner,tukfriend]]

Usually doesn't help

  • Brushing it off, or telling them to "just ignore it".
  • Checking on it all day. Agree ground rules instead.[[tukpartner]]
  • Pushing remedies, supplements or adverts. Check a claim first
  • Taking bad moods personally, especially in the early months.[[tukfriend]]

This list is our summary of charity guidance and small studies. In one study, more dismissive or punishing responses from a spouse went with more tinnitus disability.[[sullivan]]

sections.title: Around the house
sections.html:
• Bedtime sound you can both live with. A pillow speaker plays sound only for the person lying on it.[[tukpartner,tuksound]] Some couples sleep apart on bad nights or for a while. There's no research either way, so talk it through kindly so neither of you feels pushed away. Sleep and difficult nights
  • TV: turn on subtitles. A TV listener lets one person choose their own volume while the TV plays for everyone else, and a TV streamer sends sound straight to compatible hearing aids.[[rnidtv]]
  • Talking: face each other, speak clearly without shouting, rephrase rather than repeat, and turn down background noise at meals.[[rnidcomm]]
  • If you notice the TV creeping up or missed words, gently suggest a hearing check.[[nhs]] Prepare for your appointment

sections.title: Getting help can help the whole household
sections.html:
• Talking therapy. CBT, the best-supported help for tinnitus distress, can make tinnitus easier to live with. In one early study, family members felt less burdened after the person did online CBT, although it had no comparison group.[[beukes24]] CBT: the evidence
  • Support groups often welcome family and friends.[[tukpartner]] Support organizations
  • Counselling together can help if tensions are hard to manage.[[tukpartner]]

sections.title: Children and teenagers
sections.html:
Explaining a parent's tinnitus (our suggestion): "Sometimes my ears make a noise only I can hear. It isn't dangerous, and it's nobody's fault. Some days it makes me tired, and that isn't about you."

If your child has tinnitus: it's common in children, most aren't troubled by it, and a simple explanation and some reassurance is usually enough. Ask them about it gently.[[tukparents]] See a doctor if they're distressed, or have ear pain, a blocked feeling, dizziness or hearing loss. Tinnitus that beats with the pulse should always be checked.[[tukparents]]

sections.title: If you're worried about their mood or safety
sections.html:
If you think they might be thinking about suicide, it's OK to ask them directly and kindly. Asking doesn't put the idea in their head; it gives them a chance to talk.[[samaritans,nimh]]

  • Listen, and take what they say seriously. You don't have to fix it.[[samaritans]]
  • Help them connect with support: a crisis line, their doctor, or someone they trust.[[nimh]] Crisis lines by country
  • If they are in immediate danger, call your emergency number and don't leave them alone.[[nimh]]
  • Keep in touch afterwards.[[nimh]]

Supporting someone can be hard. Look after yourself too, and you can call a crisis line for advice about someone else.[[samaritans]] When it feels like too much is written for the person with tinnitus.

sections.title: Your household plan

Agree our ground rules, and a 'bad day' code word
Find a bedtime sound we can both live with

Know where to find support

sound-sensitivity.tileDesc: When sounds feel too loud, and protecting your ears
sound-sensitivity.title: Sound sensitivity and hearing protection
sound-sensitivity.metaTitle: Hyperacusis and Hearing Protection: When Sounds Feel Too Loud | Tinnitus Evidence
sound-sensitivity.metaDesc: Everyday sounds too loud or painful? How to protect your ears without over-protecting, how to fit earplugs, iPhone settings, help that works, and when to get checked.
sound-sensitivity.lead: Many people with tinnitus also find some everyday sounds too loud or uncomfortable.[[cederroth]] It's tempting to block everything out, but over-protecting your ears can make sensitivity worse.[[nhs_hyper]] The aim is to protect your ears from truly loud sound, and gently get used to everyday sound again.
now: Keep earplugs for genuinely loud things, such as power tools, concerts and motorbikes. A simple test: if you'd have to shout to be heard by someone an arm's length away, protect your ears.[[niosh]]
Leave them out for everyday sounds like the kitchen, the supermarket or traffic. Wearing earplugs all the time can make you more sensitive to sound.[[nhs_hyper,tukhyper]]
Have gentle sound around you, such as quiet music or a fan, rather than silence.[[nhs_hyper]]
Remember: uncomfortable isn't the same as harmful. Sounds below about 70 dB, like normal conversation, are unlikely to damage hearing, even over long periods.[[nidcd_nihl]]
Step away rather than plugging up when a sound is too much, and come back when you're ready.
sound-sensitivity.nowFoot: Severe ear pain with a rash, fluid coming from the ear, or a sudden change in hearing? Get checked today

sections.title: What's going on?
sections.html:
Hyperacusis means everyday sounds seem much louder than they should, or even painful.[[nhs_hyper]] Misophonia is different: strong anger, disgust or anxiety at particular sounds, often other people chewing or breathing, whatever their volume.[[swedo]] The two can overlap, and both can come with tinnitus.[[tukhyper]]

In a large Swedish study, more than half of people with tinnitus said some sounds were too loud or uncomfortable. Only about 1 in 10 had a severe problem.[[cederroth]]

sections.title: Protect, or don't plug?
sections.html:
Protect your ears

Power tools, mowers and leaf blowers; concerts and festivals; motorbikes; fireworks; shooting; loud workplaces.[[nidcd_prot]]

Carry earplugs, and use them if you'd have to shout

Cinemas, gym classes, loud bars, sports events.[[nidcd_prot,niosh]]

Leave them out

The kitchen, the supermarket, traffic, conversation, the office.[[nhs_hyper,tukhyper]]

sections.title: Wearing foam earplugs properly
sections.html:
1. With clean hands, roll the earplug into a thin, crease-free "snake".
  2. Reach over your head and pull the top of your ear up and back.
  3. Slide the earplug in and hold it for 20 to 30 seconds while it expands.
  4. Check: your own voice should sound muffled. If cupping your hands over your ears makes things much quieter, the fit isn't right, so try again.
  5. To remove, twist it slowly.

This is the NIOSH "roll, pull, hold" method.[[niosh_rph,nidcd_prot]]

Other types: reusable earplugs, including "high-fidelity" or musician's earplugs. These turn the volume down evenly, so they suit concerts and cinemas. Earmuffs are the easiest to fit. A hearing professional can also make custom earplugs. The best type is the one you'll actually wear.[[nidcd_prot]]

sections.title: On your phone
sections.html:
• iPhone: Settings, then Sounds & Haptics, then Headphone Safety. Turn on Reduce Loud Audio to lower headphone volume above a level you choose.[[apple_hs]]
  • Keep headphone volume below about 60% of maximum.[[who]]
  • Your weekly listening budget: about 80 dB for up to 40 hours a week, 90 dB for about 4 hours, and 100 dB for about 20 minutes.[[who]]
  • A free sound level meter app from NIOSH (iPhone) gives a rough reading. Use it to check now and then, not to monitor all day.[[niosh_app]]

sections.title: Help that works
sections.html:
• An audiologist can offer hyperacusis therapy: gradually getting used to sound again, often with sound therapy and advice. Evidence for sound therapy is limited, and services vary.[[kalsoom,tukhyper]]
  • CBT that includes gradual sound exposure helped people with hyperacusis in a trial, compared with waiting for treatment.[[juris]] CBT: the evidence
  • For misophonia, group CBT helped in one good trial. Other approaches are mostly untested.[[jager]]

There's no UK professional guideline for hyperacusis yet; the British Society of Audiology says it is working on one.[[bsa]]

What to tell your audiologist

  • Which sounds bother you, where, and how much. Is it the loudness, fear, anger or pain?
  • How many hours a day you wear earplugs or ear defenders.
  • What you're avoiding, and what you'd like to get back to.
  • "Please start the hearing test quietly, and let me stop if it hurts."[[aazh]] Prepare for your appointment

sections.title: A gradual sound plan to take to your audiologist
sections.html:
1. List the everyday sounds you avoid or plug out.
  2. Put them in order, from easiest to hardest.
  3. Have low, steady background sound around you each day.
  4. Cut down earplug time step by step, starting with the easiest situations.
  5. Note your discomfort from 0 to 10, and how it changes over the weeks.
  6. Review it with your audiologist.

Based on what CBT and sound-therapy programmes use; the evidence is limited. Do this with an audiologist, not instead of one.[[juris,kalsoom]]

sections.title: When to get checked quickly
sections.intro: Most sound sensitivity can wait for a routine appointment. Get help sooner for:[[nhs,nhs_earache,nord]]

summary.emergency: weakness or drooping of the face with arm weakness or trouble speaking, sound sensitivity that started after a head injury, or severe spinning dizziness that won't settle.
summary.today: severe ear pain with a rash on or in the ear, ear pain with fluid coming out, swelling around the ear or a high temperature, earache lasting more than 2 to 3 days, or a sudden drop in hearing.
summary.soon: everyday sounds that feel too loud or painful most of the time, or sound sensitivity that is stopping you doing things.

sections.title: Protect, don't over-protect
sections.intro: Tick off what you've done. Print it if that helps.
items: Earplugs in my bag for genuinely loud places
Use the arm's-length shout test
No earplugs for everyday sounds
Gentle background sound instead of silence
Turn on Reduce Loud Audio on my phone
Ask an audiologist about hyperacusis therapy
Start my gradual sound plan

evidence.text: CBT with gradual sound exposure helped hyperacusis compared with a waiting list (60 people).[[juris]]
Group CBT helped misophonia compared with a waiting list (54 people).[[jager]]
Sound therapy for hyperacusis is widely used, but the studies are few and conflicting.[[kalsoom]]
Don't wear earplugs all the time; protect your ears from genuinely loud sound; keep listening within weekly limits.[[nhs_hyper,niosh,who]]
Short experiments in volunteers show that blocking an ear for days makes sounds seem louder, which is why over-protection may backfire.[[munro]]
The protect-or-not table, the gradual sound plan and the audiologist checklist are practical tools built from the advice above.[[tukhyper]]

social-and-travel.title: Social life, restaurants and travel
social-and-travel.metaTitle: Tinnitus and Social Life: Restaurants, Concerts and Flying | Tinnitus Evidence
social-and-travel.metaDesc: Avoiding restaurants, parties or flights because of tinnitus? Practical tips for noisy places, concerts, flying and holidays, plus a gentle plan to get back to what you enjoy.
social-and-travel.lead: Tinnitus can make noisy places and trips feel daunting, and many people start saying no to things they used to enjoy.[[tuksocial]] With a little planning, most of them are still possible.
now: Pick a calmer venue and time. Soft furnishings such as carpet, curtains and padded seats soak up noise, and off-peak times are quieter.[[tuksocial]]
Ask for the right table: a booth or the quietest area, away from the bar, speakers and kitchen. If tinnitus is in one ear, put your better ear towards your companions.[[tuksocial]]
Tell the people you're with. Tinnitus is invisible, and most people are understanding once they know.[[tuksocial]]
Keep earplugs in your pocket for genuinely loud places. Leave them out at ordinary volumes, because over-protecting can make sound sensitivity worse.[[who,nhs_hyper]]
Struggling to follow conversation? Sit where you can see faces, and ask people to rephrase rather than repeat.[[rnidtips]]
social-and-travel.nowFoot: Ringing afterwards? It often settles. Spikes and difficult days

sections.title: Restaurants, parties and the cinema
sections.html:
• Restaurants: it's fine to ask staff to turn down music that's too loud.[[tuksocial]]
  • Parties: move to a quieter room or outside, talk to one person at a time, and accept that you'll miss some of it.[[tuksocial]]
  • Cinema: films can be very loud. Take earplugs, or look for subtitled or relaxed screenings.[[tuksocial]]
  • Noise ratings: some apps and review sites show how loud venues are. Readings are rough and user-submitted, but they can help you choose.

Phone tools that can help

  • Live Listen turns an iPhone into a microphone that sends voices to your AirPods. Put the phone near the person you want to hear, and keep the volume moderate.[[apple_ll]]
  • Live Captions shows captions of speech around you on iPhone 11 or later, in some languages. Accuracy varies.[[apple_lc]]
  • If you have hearing loss, hearing aids with a remote microphone can make noisy places much easier.[[rnidtips]] Hearing aids: the evidence

You could say to friends: "I have tinnitus, a constant sound in my ears. Noisy rooms make it hard to follow conversation. If I lean in or ask you to repeat, that's why. A quieter table really helps."

When booking: "Could we have a booth, or a table away from the speakers and kitchen? I have a hearing condition."

sections.title: Concerts, festivals and loud events
sections.html:
• Wear earplugs. Filtered earplugs turn the volume down without muffling the music.[[tuksocial]] In a festival trial, earplugs cut new tinnitus after the event from 40% to 12%.[[ramakers]]
  • Stay away from the speakers. Sound drops quickly with distance.[[who]]
  • Take a 10-minute quiet break every hour.[[who]]
  • Ringing afterwards often fades. If it doesn't, or your hearing still feels muffled after a day or two, get it checked.[[who,nhs]] When to get help quickly

sections.title: Flying
sections.html:
Most people with tinnitus have no problems flying, and any effect is usually minor and temporary.[[tukfly]]

  • Help your ears with the pressure: swallow, yawn, chew gum or suck a sweet, especially as you come in to land, and try to stay awake for the descent.[[tukfly,enthealth]] Pinching your nose and blowing very gently can help too; never force it.[[enthealth]]
  • Try not to fly with a heavy cold. Ask a pharmacist about decongestants, which aren't suitable for everyone.[[tukfly,enthealth]]
  • Keep your hearing aids in.[[tukfly]]
  • Don't seal out all sound with earplugs, because it can make tinnitus more noticeable. If engine noise bothers you, sit in front of the wings.[[tukfly]] Noise-cancelling headphones are fine at a low volume with something pleasant playing.[[who]]
  • Pressure-regulating earplugs are widely sold, but there's little evidence they help.[[ryan]]
  • Had ear surgery? Check with your specialist before flying.[[tukfly]]

sections.title: Holidays and travel
sections.html:
• Pack your bedtime sound: a phone app, a small speaker or a fan setting, so unfamiliar quiet rooms are easier.[[tuksound]]
  • Jet lag: shift your sleep times gradually before you go, get daylight when you arrive, and avoid naps.[[nhs_jetlag]] Sleep and difficult nights
  • Airport security (US): you don't have to remove hearing aids or cochlear implants.[[tsa]]
  • Travel insurance: declare existing health conditions, and check with your insurer whether to list tinnitus.[[govuk_ins]]
  • Diving: new tinnitus during or after a dive needs a prompt medical check. Ask a diving doctor before diving with existing tinnitus if you're unsure.[[dan]]

sections.title: Getting back to things you've stopped
sections.html:
Avoiding things brings quick relief, but over time it can keep worry about tinnitus going.[[cima18,kleinstauber]] A gentle, step-by-step plan can help you get back to what matters:

  1. List what you've stopped doing because of tinnitus.
  2. Put them in order, from easiest to hardest.
  3. Start with a short, easy version, such as a quiet café mid-afternoon for 30 minutes.
  4. Stay until the worry eases a little, rather than leaving at the first discomfort.
  5. Afterwards, compare what happened with what you expected.
  6. Repeat, then move up a step.

No trial has tested this exact plan for social life with tinnitus; it uses the same approach as CBT.[[cima18]] If the anxiety feels bigger than you can manage, try it with a CBT practitioner. When it feels like too much

sections.title: Your going-out checklist
sections.intro: Tick off what helps you. Save or print it for next time.
items: Choose a venue with soft furnishings, at a quieter time
Ask for a booth or a table away from speakers, bar and kitchen
Tell my friends what helps

Phone charged for Live Listen or captions, if I use them
A 10-minute quiet break every hour at loud events
Bedtime sound packed for travel
One small step back towards something I've stopped doing

evidence.text: Avoidance and fear of tinnitus go with more distress and disability; CBT works partly by reducing them.[[cima18,kleinstauber]]
Earplugs at a music festival reduced new tinnitus afterwards (12% vs 40%).[[ramakers]]
A systematic review found too little evidence that pressure-regulating earplugs prevent ear problems when flying.[[ryan]]
Safe listening at loud events: distance from speakers, hourly breaks, earplugs.[[who]]
Venue choice, seating, scripts, flying tips and the step-by-step plan are expert advice from tinnitus and hearing charities, with little direct research.[[tuksocial,tukfly,rnidtips]]
